subject: Mathematics
title: The Village Path Blueprint
hook: A surveyor maps village paths—learn the math behind straight lines and angles.

characters.name: Meena
characters.role: Local farmer interested in land division

slides.title: Straight Lines: Mapping the Village Path
slides.storyContext: Surveyor Sharma must map new paths between the village well (at 2,3) and the temple (at 8,9) on a coordinate grid. Arjun asks: how do we describe this path mathematically?
slides.inSimpleWords: A straight line on a coordinate plane can be described with equations and slopes.

slides.title: The Well and the Temple
slides.storyContext: Arjun holds the surveyor's chain as Surveyor Sharma plots coordinates. 'The well is at grid (2,3). The temple is at (8,9),' Sharma explains. 'To find the path, we need to know the direction—how steep is the climb? And where does the path cross the well's baseline?' Arjun sketches on paper. 'Is there a formula?' Sharma nods. 'Yes—we call it the slope-intercept form.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Every straight line has a slope (steepness) and a y-intercept (where it crosses the y-axis).

slides.title: Slope of a Line

points.label: Definition
points.text: Slope m = (y₂ - y₁)/(x₂ - x₁). It measures how steep a line is.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: m > 0: line rises (northeast). m < 0: line falls (southeast). m = 0: horizontal. m undefined: vertical.

points.label: Well to Temple
points.text: Points (2,3) and (8,9). Slope m = (9-3)/(8-2) = 6/6 = 1. The path rises at a 45° angle.

example.problem: A farmer walks from point (1,2) to point (4,8). What is the slope of the path?
example.solution: m = (8-2)/(4-1) = 6/3 = 2. The path rises 2 units for every 1 unit walked horizontally.

slides.inSimpleWords: Slope tells you how fast a line rises or falls—steeper slope means a sharper climb.

slides.title: Worked Example: Slope Through Practice
slides.storyContext: Meena's farmland runs from point A(0,1) to point B(5,11). What slope describes the farm's boundary line?

points.label: Apply Slope Formula
points.text: m = (11-1)/(5-0) = 10/5 = 2. For every 1 meter east, the boundary rises 2 meters north.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: A slope of 2 means a fairly steep climb. This boundary line tilts significantly upward.

slides.inSimpleWords: Practice calculating slopes with real farm coordinates—always subtract in the same order.

slides.title: Equation of a Line: Slope-Intercept Form

points.label: Form
points.text: y = mx + c, where m is slope and c is the y-intercept (where line crosses y-axis).

points.label: Finding c
points.text: Using the well-temple line: slope m = 1, point (2,3). Substitute: 3 = 1(2) + c → c = 1.

points.label: Final Equation
points.text: The path line is y = x + 1. Any point (x,y) on this path satisfies this equation.

example.problem: A road passes through (3,5) with slope 2. Find its equation.
example.solution: y = mx + c. Using (3,5): 5 = 2(3) + c → c = -1. Equation: y = 2x - 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: The equation y = mx + c is the universal formula for any straight line.

slides.title: Worked Example: Building the Line Equation
slides.storyContext: Arjun records that Surveyor Sharma's mapping line passes through (1,4) with slope 3. What's the equation of this survey line?

points.label: Use Point-Slope
points.text: Given: point (1,4), slope m = 3. Formula y = mx + c becomes 4 = 3(1) + c.

points.label: Solve for c
points.text: 4 = 3 + c → c = 1. The y-intercept is 1.

points.label: Final Equation
points.text: y = 3x + 1. Any coordinate on this survey line satisfies this equation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Once you know slope and one point, you can write the complete line equation.

slides.title: Two-Point Form and General Form

points.label: Two-Point Form
points.text: (y - y₁)/(x - x₁) = (y₂ - y₁)/(x₂ - x₁). Use this when you have two points.

points.label: General Form
points.text: Ax + By + C = 0. Example: x - y + 1 = 0 is the well-temple line rearranged.

points.label: Intercept Form
points.text: x/a + y/b = 1, where a is x-intercept and b is y-intercept. Useful for axes crossings.

example.problem: Write the equation of the line through (0,4) and (2,0).
example.solution: Intercept form: x/2 + y/4 = 1, or 2x + y = 4. General form: 2x + y - 4 = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different forms of line equations serve different situations—pick the form that fits your data.

slides.title: Worked Example: General Form from Two Points
slides.storyContext: Meena needs to write the boundary line through villages at (1,3) and (4,9) in general form Ax + By + C = 0.

points.label: Convert to General Form
points.text: y = 2x + 1 → 2x - y + 1 = 0. This is the general form Ax + By + C = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Start with slope-intercept, then rearrange to general form when needed for calculations.

slides.title: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines

points.label: Parallel Lines
points.text: Two lines are parallel if they have the same slope: m₁ = m₂. They never meet.

points.label: Perpendicular Lines
points.text: Two lines are perpendicular if m₁ × m₂ = -1. Example: if m₁ = 2, then m₂ = -1/2.

points.label: Village Application
points.text: The path y = x + 1 is perpendicular to y = -x + 5 (slopes: 1 and -1, product = -1).

example.problem: Find a line parallel to y = 3x + 2 passing through (1,5).
example.solution: Parallel means same slope m = 3. Using y = 3x + c: 5 = 3(1) + c → c = 2. Answer: y = 3x + 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines have same slope; perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is -1.

slides.title: Worked Example: Perpendicular Lines in Practice
slides.storyContext: A water channel must be perpendicular to the main path y = 2x + 1 and pass through the well at (2,3). Find the channel's equation.

points.label: Find Perpendicular Slope
points.text: Main path slope m₁ = 2. Perpendicular slope m₂ satisfies 2 × m₂ = -1 → m₂ = -1/2.

points.label: Use Point and Slope
points.text: Channel passes through (2,3) with m = -1/2. So 3 = (-1/2)(2) + c → 3 = -1 + c → c = 4.

points.label: Channel Equation
points.text: y = -x/2 + 4 or x + 2y - 8 = 0. Water flows at 90° to the main path.

slides.inSimpleWords: To build perpendicular structures, multiply slopes by -1 and divide: one gives you the other.

slides.title: Distance from a Point to a Line

points.label: Distance Formula
points.text: Distance from point (x₀,y₀) to line Ax + By + C = 0 is d = |Ax₀ + By₀ + C|/√(A² + B²).

points.label: Use Case
points.text: How far is Meena's farm at (5,7) from the path-line x - y + 1 = 0?

example.problem: Find the distance from (2,3) to the line 3x + 4y - 5 = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance formula helps measure shortest separation between a point and a line.

slides.title: Worked Example: Measuring Distance to Survey Line
slides.storyContext: Arjun checks how far the well at (1,2) is from the surveyor's main line 2x - 3y + 4 = 0.

points.label: Identify Values
points.text: Point: (x₀,y₀) = (1,2). Line: A=2, B=-3, C=4.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: The well lies exactly ON the survey line (distance = 0), so it's perfectly aligned with the surveyor's path.

slides.inSimpleWords: Check if a point is on a line: if distance = 0, the point is exactly on the line.

slides.title: Intersection Points and Angle Between Lines
slides.storyContext: Surveyor Sharma points to where two paths cross in the village. 'Two lines intersect at exactly one point—unless they're parallel,' he explains. 'And we can measure the angle between them using their slopes.' Meena sketches: 'So slopes tell us not just direction, but also the angle of intersection?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Where two lines cross is their intersection point; the angle between them depends on their slopes.

slides.title: Full Problem: Mapping Two Farm Boundaries
slides.storyContext: Surveyor Sharma must find where two farm boundaries meet. Farm A's edge: y = 2x + 3. Farm B's edge: y = -x + 9. Where do they intersect?

points.label: Set Equal
points.text: At intersection, y values are equal: 2x + 3 = -x + 9.

points.label: Find y
points.text: y = 2(2) + 3 = 7. Intersection at (2,7).

slides.inSimpleWords: To find where two lines meet, solve their equations simultaneously.

slides.title: Angle Between Two Lines

points.label: Formula
points.text: tan(θ) = |(m₁ - m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|, where m₁ and m₂ are the slopes.

points.label: Special Cases
points.text: If 1 + m₁m₂ = 0, then m₁m₂ = -1 (perpendicular, θ = 90°). If m₁ = m₂, then θ = 0° (parallel).

example.problem: Find the angle between y = x + 2 and y = 2x + 3.

slides.inSimpleWords: The angle between two lines is determined entirely by their slopes.

slides.title: Worked Example: Angle Between Farm Boundaries
slides.storyContext: At the intersection point (2,7), what angle do the two farm boundaries make? (A: y = 2x+3, B: y = -x+9)

points.label: Identify Slopes
points.text: Farm A: m₁ = 2. Farm B: m₂ = -1.

points.label: Find Angle
points.text: θ = arctan(3) ≈ 71.57°. The boundaries meet at approximately 71.6 degrees.

slides.inSimpleWords: Verify perpendicularity: if the product of slopes is -1, the angle is always 90°.

slides.title: Challenge: Parallel Farm Paths
slides.storyContext: Meena wants a new boundary line parallel to y = (1/2)x + 3 passing through her barn at (6,2). Write the equation and convert it to general form.

example.problem: Find a line parallel to y = (1/2)x + 3 through (6,2), then write in general form.

slides.inSimpleWords: Practice finding parallel lines—they have identical slopes but different y-intercepts.

slides.title: Challenge: Distance to Boundary
slides.storyContext: Calculate how far Meena's house at (3,4) is from the boundary line 3x + 4y - 12 = 0.

example.problem: Find distance from (3,4) to line 3x + 4y - 12 = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always use absolute value in the numerator to get a positive distance.

slides.title: Challenge: Finding Intersection Points
slides.storyContext: Two village paths are y = 3x - 2 and y = -2x + 8. Find their intersection and the angle between them.

example.problem: Find intersection and angle for y = 3x - 2 and y = -2x + 8.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine intersection and angle concepts: solve for x-y, then use slope formula for angle.

slides.title: Straight Lines Summary

points.text: Slope m = Δy/Δx. It measures line steepness and direction.
Equations: y = mx + c (slope-intercept), Ax + By + C = 0 (general), x/a + y/b = 1 (intercept).
Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes with product -1.
Distance from point to line: d = |Ax₀ + By₀ + C|/√(A² + B²).
Angle between lines: tan(θ) = |(m₁ - m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)| at their intersection.
Applications: surveying lands, designing roads, planning buildings, farm boundaries, navigation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Straight line equations are the foundation of coordinate geometry—used in architecture, surveying, and engineering.

subject: Mathematics
title: The Mirror and the Curve
hook: A satellite dish, a bridge arch, and a planet's orbit—all follow conic section curves.

slides.title: Conic Sections: Circles, Ellipses, Parabolas, Hyperbolas
slides.storyContext: When light rays are cut by a cone at different angles, they create curves used everywhere: satellite dishes, bridge arches, planets' orbits, and water fountains.
slides.inSimpleWords: Conic sections are curves made by slicing a cone—each has unique properties and equations.

image.alt: Conic Sections: Circles, Ellipses, Parabolas, Hyperbolas — Conic Sections

slides.title: The Fountain Challenge
slides.storyContext: Govind is designing a water fountain for the village square. The water jets must follow a perfect arch—not too steep, not too flat. Ravi says, 'That's a parabola!' Govind nods: 'Yes, and I need its equation to calculate flow rates.' Diya adds, 'Parabolas appear in satellites too—they focus signals to a receiver.' All three realize conics are everywhere.
slides.inSimpleWords: Conic sections model real-world curves from engineering to astronomy.

slides.title: Circle: The Perfect Curve

points.label: Definition
points.text: A circle is the set of all points equidistant from a center. Distance = radius r.

points.label: Standard Equation
points.text: (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r², where (h,k) is center and r is radius.

points.label: General Equation
points.text: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0. Center = (-g, -f), radius = √(g² + f² - c).

example.problem: A circular well has center at (2,3) and radius 5. Write its equation.
example.solution: (x - 2)² + (y - 3)² = 25. Expanding: x² + y² - 4x - 6y - 12 = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: A circle is defined by one center point and a radius—the simplest conic section.

slides.title: Worked Example: Circle from General Form
slides.storyContext: Ravi records a circular orbit described by x² + y² - 6x - 8y = 0. Find the center and radius.

points.label: Group Terms
points.text: (x² - 6x) + (y² - 8y) = 0. Complete the square for each variable.

points.label: Extract Info
points.text: Center (3,4), radius = 5 units. This circular orbit has its center 3 units east and 4 units north.

slides.inSimpleWords: To find center and radius from general form, complete the square and compare to standard form.

slides.title: Parabola: The Arch of Motion

points.label: Definition
points.text: A parabola is the set of points equidistant from a focus F and a directrix line.

points.label: Standard Equation (Vertex at origin)
points.text: y² = 4ax (opens right) or x² = 4ay (opens up). Here a is distance from vertex to focus.

points.label: Fountain Example
points.text: Water jet equation x² = 4(1.25)y = 5y. Focus at (0, 1.25), directrix at y = -1.25.

example.problem: A water fountain parabola is x² = 8y. Find focus and directrix.
example.solution: 4a = 8 → a = 2. Focus at (0, 2). Directrix: y = -2. Water rises symmetrically from the center.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parabolas are perfect arches used in water fountains, bridge cables, and satellite dishes.

slides.title: Worked Example: Finding Focus of Parabola
slides.storyContext: Govind's fountain design follows y² = 12x. Where is the receiver at the focus?

points.label: Identify Form
points.text: This is y² = 4ax form, opening rightward (horizontal).

points.label: Locate Focus
points.text: Focus at (a, 0) = (3, 0). Directrix is the line x = -3. The receiver is 3 units to the right of the vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: For parabola y² = 4ax, the focus is always at distance a from the vertex along the axis.

slides.title: Ellipse: The Stretched Circle

points.label: Definition
points.text: An ellipse is the set of points where sum of distances to two foci = constant (2a).

points.label: Standard Equation
points.text: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 (a ≥ b). Semi-major axis = a, semi-minor axis = b.

points.label: Foci and Eccentricity
points.text: Foci at (±c, 0) where c² = a² - b². Eccentricity e = c/a (0 < e < 1).

example.problem: A planet's orbit is x²/100 + y²/64 = 1 (in million km). Find semi-major axis, semi-minor axis, and foci.
example.solution: a = 10, b = 8. c² = 100 - 64 = 36 → c = 6. Foci at (±6, 0). Semi-major = 10, semi-minor = 8.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ellipses describe planetary orbits and stretched circular paths—essential to astronomy.

slides.title: Worked Example: Ellipse Eccentricity
slides.storyContext: Diya studies an asteroid orbit: x²/49 + y²/24 = 1. How stretched is this ellipse?

points.label: Identify Parameters
points.text: a² = 49 → a = 7 (semi-major). b² = 24 → b ≈ 4.9 (semi-minor).

points.label: Find Eccentricity
points.text: e = c/a = 5/7 ≈ 0.714. This ellipse is fairly stretched (close to 1 means very elongated).

slides.inSimpleWords: Eccentricity measures how much an ellipse stretches: e=0 is a circle, e close to 1 is very elongated.

slides.title: Hyperbola: The Twin Curves

points.label: Definition
points.text: A hyperbola is the set of points where |difference of distances| to two foci = constant (2a).

points.label: Standard Equation
points.text: x²/a² - y²/b² = 1 (opens left-right). Foci at (±c, 0) where c² = a² + b².

points.label: Asymptotes
points.text: Lines y = ±(b/a)x. Hyperbola approaches these lines but never crosses.

example.problem: Write the equation of a hyperbola with foci at (±5, 0) and difference of distances = 6.

slides.inSimpleWords: Hyperbolas are two mirrored curves that approach asymptotes—used in radar and navigation.

image.alt: Hyperbola: The Twin Curves — Conic Sections

slides.title: Worked Example: Hyperbola Asymptotes
slides.storyContext: A navigation system uses the hyperbola x²/25 - y²/16 = 1. What are its asymptotes?

points.label: Identify Hyperbola Type
points.text: This opens left-right (x² positive first). So a² = 25 → a = 5, b² = 16 → b = 4.

points.label: Asymptote Formula
points.text: For x²/a² - y²/b² = 1, asymptotes are y = ±(b/a)x = ±(4/5)x.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: The hyperbola gets closer and closer to lines y = 0.8x and y = -0.8x as x increases.

slides.inSimpleWords: Asymptotes guide the shape of hyperbolas—they're the 'rails' the curves follow at infinity.

slides.title: Real-World Applications of Conics

points.label: Parabola
points.text: Satellite dishes, water fountains, bridge arches, projectile motion (cricket ball trajectory).

points.label: Ellipse
points.text: Planetary orbits (Kepler's 1st law), whispering galleries (sound focuses), swimming pools.

points.label: Hyperbola
points.text: Radio towers (hyperbolic reflectors), GPS systems, nuclear cooling towers.

points.label: Circle
points.text: Wheels, orbits (special case of ellipse), architectural designs, wheels on carts.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every conic section solves real problems—from designing buildings to tracking satellites.

slides.title: Full Problem: The Bridge Arch
slides.storyContext: An engineer designs a bridge with a parabolic arch. The arch spans 40 meters horizontally and rises 10 meters at the center. Write the equation.

points.label: Set up coordinates
points.text: Vertex at origin (0,0). Left end at (-20,-10), right end at (20,-10). Opening downward: x² = -4ay.

points.label: Equation
points.text: x² = -40y or y = -x²/40. This describes the bridge's perfect arch.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real bridge arches are parabolas—calculated to support weight evenly across the span.

image.alt: Full Problem: The Bridge Arch — Conic Sections

slides.title: Challenge: Satellite Dish Focus
slides.storyContext: A satellite receiver is designed as a parabolic mirror y² = 16x. A signal receiver sits at the focus. Find the focus coordinates.

example.problem: For the parabola y² = 16x, find the focus.
example.solution: Form y² = 4ax. Here 4a = 16 → a = 4. Focus at (4, 0). All signals parallel to the axis reflect to this point.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parabolic mirrors focus parallel rays to a single point—the key to powerful receivers.

slides.title: Challenge: Elliptical Pool Design
slides.storyContext: A swimming pool has elliptical shape x²/100 + y²/64 = 1 (in meters). Find the major and minor axis lengths.

example.problem: For ellipse x²/100 + y²/64 = 1, find major and minor axis lengths.
example.solution: a² = 100 → a = 10 (semi-major). b² = 64 → b = 8 (semi-minor). Major axis = 2a = 20 m, Minor axis = 2b = 16 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Pool designers use ellipses for elegant curves—the major and minor axes determine overall dimensions.

slides.title: Conic Sections Summary

points.text: Circle: (x-h)² + (y-k)² = r². All points equidistant from center.
Parabola: y² = 4ax or x² = 4ay. Equidistant from focus and directrix. Used in dishes, fountains, arches.
Ellipse: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1. Sum of distances to foci is constant. Describes planetary orbits.
Hyperbola: x²/a² - y²/b² = 1. Difference of distances to foci is constant. Used in navigation.
Every conic has eccentricity e: circle (e=0), ellipse (0<e<1), parabola (e=1), hyperbola (e>1).

slides.inSimpleWords: Conic sections are the foundation of orbital mechanics, optics, and architectural design.

subject: Mathematics
title: Building in Three Dimensions
hook: From flat paper to real buildings—learn to navigate and measure in 3D space.

slides.title: 3D Geometry: Building in Three Dimensions
slides.storyContext: Architect Patel must design a new school building. The design requires coordinates in 3D: length, width, and height. Ankit asks, 'How do we describe positions in 3D space?'
slides.inSimpleWords: In 3D space, every point needs three coordinates (x, y, z)—length, width, and height.

image.alt: 3D Geometry: Building in Three Dimensions — Introduction to Three Dimensional Geometry

slides.title: From 2D Drawings to 3D Reality
slides.storyContext: Ankit holds the architect's blueprint. 'On the drawing, the door is at (2,3)—that's flat,' says Patel. 'But in the real building, we must say (2,3,0) for ground level, or (2,3,1.5) if it's on the wall. We need a third coordinate for height.' Priya sketches: 'So (x,y,z) describes any point in the building?' Patel nods. 'Exactly. Let's master 3D coordinates.'
slides.inSimpleWords: The 3D coordinate system extends 2D coordinates by adding height as the z-axis.

slides.title: The 3D Coordinate System

points.label: Three Axes
points.text: x-axis (length), y-axis (width), z-axis (height). They meet at origin O(0,0,0).

points.label: Octants
points.text: 3D space divides into 8 octants, like quadrants in 2D but in 3D.

points.label: Point Representation
points.text: Any point P in 3D is (x, y, z). Example: a door handle at (2, 3, 1.8) meters.

example.problem: Locate the corner of a room at (4, 6, 0). What is its position relative to the origin?
example.solution: 4 meters along x-axis, 6 meters along y-axis, ground level (z=0). This is where a wall meets another wall on the floor.

slides.inSimpleWords: The 3D coordinate system uses three perpendicular axes to locate any point in space.

slides.title: Worked Example: Identifying 3D Coordinates
slides.storyContext: Ankit points out three key building points: (0,0,0) at the entrance, (5,0,0) at the far wall, and (5,5,3) at the roof corner. Plot them mentally.

points.label: Entrance Point
points.text: (0,0,0) is the origin—right at the corner where two walls meet at ground level.

points.label: Far Wall Point
points.text: (5,0,0) is 5 meters along the x-axis, ground level—on the far wall.

points.label: Roof Corner Point
points.text: (5,5,3) is 5 meters along x, 5 meters along y, and 3 meters high—this is a corner of the roof.

slides.inSimpleWords: Picture each coordinate: the x-value steps right, y-value steps forward, z-value steps up.

slides.title: Distance Between Two Points in 3D

points.label: Distance Formula
points.text: Distance AB = √((x₂-x₁)² + (y₂-y₁)² + (z₂-z₁)²)

points.label: Building Application
points.text: From ground door (2,3,0) to roof corner (5,8,10), distance = √((5-2)² + (8-3)² + (10-0)²) = √(9+25+100) = √134 ≈ 11.6 meters.

points.label: Pythagoras in 3D
points.text: The formula extends Pythagorean theorem to three dimensions.

example.problem: Find the distance from room corner (1,2,3) to ceiling point (4,6,5).

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D distance formula is like the 2D Pythagorean theorem, but with a third dimension added.

slides.title: Worked Example: Calculating Diagonal Distance
slides.storyContext: Priya measures the diagonal through a room from corner (0,0,0) to opposite corner (6,8,3). What's the room's diagonal length?

points.label: Calculate Result
points.text: √109 ≈ 10.44 meters. The room's body diagonal is about 10.44 meters long.

points.label: Verification
points.text: This is longer than any single side (6, 8, or 3) because it's a diagonal through 3D space.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always square each coordinate difference, sum them, then take the square root.

slides.title: Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios

points.label: Direction Ratios
points.text: For vector from A(x₁,y₁,z₁) to B(x₂,y₂,z₂): direction ratios are (a,b,c) = (x₂-x₁, y₂-y₁, z₂-z₁).

points.label: Direction Cosines
points.text: l = a/d, m = b/d, n = c/d, where d = √(a²+b²+c²) is the distance. Note: l² + m² + n² = 1.

points.label: Building Example
points.text: From (2,3,0) to (5,8,10), ratios are (3,5,10). Distance d = √134. Cosines: l≈0.26, m≈0.43, n≈0.87.

example.problem: Find direction cosines from A(0,0,0) to B(1,1,1).
example.solution: Ratios: (1,1,1). Distance: √3. Cosines: l = 1/√3, m = 1/√3, n = 1/√3. Each ≈ 0.577.

slides.inSimpleWords: Direction cosines describe how a line is oriented in 3D space—useful for architectural slopes.

slides.title: Worked Example: Direction Cosines Calculation
slides.storyContext: A support beam runs from (1,2,2) to (4,6,5). What are its direction cosines?
slides.inSimpleWords: Direction cosines always sum to 1 (when squared)—a useful check on calculations.

slides.title: Section Formula: Dividing a Line Segment

points.label: Internal Division
points.text: Point P divides line AB in ratio m:n. Then P = ((m·x₂ + n·x₁)/(m+n), (m·y₂ + n·y₁)/(m+n), (m·z₂ + n·z₁)/(m+n)).

points.label: Midpoint (1:1 ratio)
points.text: Midpoint M = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2, (z₁+z₂)/2).

points.label: Application
points.text: Architects use this to locate structural supports: if a beam runs from (0,0,0) to (10,10,10), support at 2:1 point is at (20/3, 20/3, 20/3) ≈ (6.67, 6.67, 6.67).

example.problem: Find point P dividing segment from A(1,2,3) to B(7,8,9) in ratio 2:1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Section formula helps locate structural points along beams and construction lines.

slides.title: Worked Example: Midpoint in 3D
slides.storyContext: A building's main diagonal runs from (0,0,0) to (12,10,8). Find the center point of this diagonal.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: The building's center is at (6, 5, 4) meters—exactly halfway through the diagonal.

slides.inSimpleWords: Midpoint is the simplest case of section formula—dividing a segment into two equal parts.

slides.title: Equation of a Line in 3D

points.label: Parametric Form
points.text: Line through point A(a,b,c) with direction (l,m,n): x = a + lt, y = b + mt, z = c + nt, where t is parameter.

points.label: Wall Edge Example
points.text: Wall edge from (0,0,0) to (0,5,3) has parametric: x=0, y=5t, z=3t. At t=0: (0,0,0); at t=1: (0,5,3).

example.problem: Write parametric equations for a line through (2,3,4) with direction (1,2,3).

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D line equations use parameters (t) to describe every point along the line.

slides.title: Worked Example: Parametric Line from Two Points
slides.storyContext: A cable runs between two building points: (1,1,2) and (5,7,8). Write the parametric equations.

points.label: Write Parametric Equations
points.text: Using point (1,1,2): x = 1 + 4t, y = 1 + 6t, z = 2 + 6t.

points.label: Verify
points.text: At t=0: (1,1,2). At t=1: (5,7,8). The cable is traced as t goes from 0 to 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Start at a point, then add direction components scaled by parameter t—this traces the entire line.

slides.title: Full Problem: The Diagonal Beam
slides.storyContext: Architect Patel designs a diagonal support beam from corner A(0,0,0) to opposite corner B(10,8,6) of a building. Find the beam's length and the point exactly halfway along.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: The beam is 14.14 meters long. The midpoint (5,4,3) is where the architect plans a structural support.

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D distance and section formulas are essential for structural engineering and construction planning.

slides.title: Challenge: Rooftop Antenna Length
slides.storyContext: An antenna is placed at (5, 4, 12)—on the roof corner at height 12m. The base of the antenna pole is at (5, 4, 0). Find the antenna's length and direction cosines.

example.problem: From (5,4,0) to (5,4,12), find length and direction cosines.
example.solution: Length: √((5-5)² + (4-4)² + (12-0)²) = √144 = 12 meters. Direction ratios: (0,0,12). Direction cosines: l=0, m=0, n=1 (points straight up).

slides.inSimpleWords: Vertical structures like antennas have simple direction cosines—all the cosine goes to n.

slides.inSimpleWords: Section formula divides lines unequally—useful for placing supports not at the midpoint.

slides.title: 3D Geometry Summary

points.text: 3D coordinates (x,y,z) locate points in space using three perpendicular axes.
Distance: d = √((x₂-x₁)² + (y₂-y₁)² + (z₂-z₁)²).
Direction cosines (l,m,n) describe line orientation; l² + m² + n² = 1.
Section formula divides a segment in any ratio; midpoint is the 1:1 case.
Line in 3D: parametric form (x,y,z) = (a,b,c) + t(l,m,n) or symmetric form.
Applications: architecture, construction, surveying, navigation, computer graphics.

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D geometry extends 2D coordinate ideas to the real world—essential for building and design.
